Not as with you, Thou loathſome ſtrumpet: ſome good pittying Man Remoue my ſinnes out of my ſight a little, I tremble to behold her, ſhe keepes backe All comfort while ſhe ſtayes, is this a time, Vnconſcionable Woman, to ſee thee, Art thou ſo cruell to the peace of Man, Not to giue libertie now, the Diuell himſelfe Shewes a farre fairer reuerence and reſpect To goodneſſe then thy ſelfe, he dares not doe this, But part in time of penitence, hides his Face, When Man with-drawes from him, he leaues the place, Haſt thou leſſe manners, and more impudence, Then thy inſtructer, prethee ſhew thy modeſtie, If the leaſt graine be left, and get thee from me, Thou ſhould'ſt be rather lock't many Roomes hence, From the poore miſerable ſight of me ▪ If either loue or grace had part in thee. O Death! Is this A place for you to weepe? What teares are thoſe? Get you away with them, I ſhall fare the worſe, As long as they are a weeping, they worke againſt me, There's nothing but thy appetite in that ſorrow, Thou weep'ſt for Luſt, I feele it in the ſlackneſſe Of comforts comming towards me, I was well till thou began'ſt to vndoe me, This ſhewes like the fruitleſſe ſorrow of a careleſſe mother That brings her Sonne with dalliance to the Gallowes, And then ſtands by, and weepes to ſee him ſuffer. O my vengeance, let me for euer hide my curſed Face From ſight of thoſe that darkens all my hopes, And ſtands betweene me and the ſight of Heauen, Who ſees me now, ho to and thoſe ſo neere me, May rightly ſay, I am o're-growne with ſinne, O how my offences wraſtle with my repentance, It hath ſcarce breath, Still my adulterous guilt houers aloft, And with her blacke Wings beats downe all my prayers. Ere they be halfe way vp, what's he knowes now, How long I haue to liue? ô what comes then, My taſt growes bitter, the round World, all Gall now, Her pleaſing pleaſures now hath poyſon'd me, Which I exchang'd my Soule for, Make way a hundred ſighes at once for me. Wretched, death of ſeauen. O ſorrow! My Will? Yes, yes, what elſe? Who writes apace now? Set it downe then: Inprimis, I bequeath to yonder Witall, Three times his weight in Curſes, All Plagues of Body and of Mind, Together alſo, With ſuch a Sickneſſe, ten dayes ere his Death. Next I bequeath to that foule whore his Wife, All barrenneſſe of Ioy, a drouth of Vertue, And dearth of all repentance: For her end, The common miſerie of an Engliſh Strumpet, In French and Duch, beholding ere ſhe dyes Confuſion of her Brats before her Eyes, And neuer ſhed a teare for it. Dead? Lift, lift, Who helpes me? What's this? Am I deny'd a Chamber? What ſay you forſooth? O Death! doe I heare this with part Of former life in me? What's the newes now? Why how Sir? All ill at once. I'le ſoone ſaue you that labour. If euer Eyes were open, theſe are they, Gamſters farewell, I haue nothing left to play.

I knew 'twold pricke, Thus doe I faſhion ſtill All mine owne ends by him and his ranke toyle, 'Tis my deſire to keepe him ſtill from marriage, Being his poore neereſt Kinſman, I may fare The better at his death, there my hopes build Since my Lady Kixe is dry, and hath no Child.

Well Knight, that choyſe ſpoy is onely kept for me. Turne not to me till thou mayſt lawfully, it but whets my ſtomacke, which is too ſharpe ſet already. Read that note carefully, keepe me from ſuſpition ſtill, nor know my zeale but in thy Heart: read and ſend but thy liking in three words, I'le be at hand to take it. I muſt about it. Rather then the gaine ſhould fall to a Stranger, 'twas honeſtie in me to enrich my Father. O nothing now, all that I wiſh is preſent. So is the Miſtris. Yes ſure I thinke I haue her meaſure about me, good faith 'tis downe, I cannot ſhow't you, I muſt pull too many things out to be certaine. Let me ſee, long, and ſlender, and neatly ioynted, Iuſt ſuch another Gentlewoman that's your Daughter Sir. I proteſt I neuer ſaw two Maids handed more alike I'le nere ſeeke farther, if you'le giue me leaue Sir. I, and I'le bide all loſſe Sir. Shall I make bold with your finger Gentlewoman? That fits her to a haire Sir. Maſſe that's true, Poſie I faith eene thus Sir. Loue that's wiſe, blinds Parents Eyes. What Sir? Pardon you? I Sir. Yes faith I will. Thy doome take hold of thee. Being ſo 'tis ſoone, thankes, and your leaue ſweet Gentlewoman Brother I haue ſought you ſtrangely. With all ſpeed thou canſt procure a Licence for me. Cuds-foot ſhe's loſt elſe, I ſhall miſſe her euer. Thankes by hundreds. The hapieſt meeting that our ſoules could wiſh for Here's the Ring ready, I am beholding vnto your Fathers haſt, h'as kept his howre. Backe, be ſilent. It vowes your ſeruice Sir. Sir I obey your time. O Sir, if euer you felt the force of loue, pittie it in me. Here 'tis ready Sir. The Ring and all things perfect, ſhe'le ſteale hither. O here ſhe's come Sir. My honeſt Brother. Hard fate. And you cannot ſee with thoſe two Glaſſes, put on a paire more. I thinke you did, you receiued money for't. Like enough Sir, you ha' tane me at the worſt time for words that e're ye pick't out, faith doe not wrong me Sir. Y'are in the happieſt way to enrich your ſelfe, And pleaſure me Brother, as Mans feet can tread in, For though ſhe be lock't vp, her vow is fix't onely to me; Then time ſhall neuer grieue me, for by that vow, E'ne abſent inioy her, aſſuredly confirm'd that none Elſe ſhall, which will make tedious yeeres ſeeme gamefull To me, In the meane ſpace loſe you no time ſweet brother, You haue the meanes to ſtrike at this Knights fortunes, And lay him leuell with his bankrout merit, Get but his Wife with Child, perch at tree top, And ſhake the golden fruit into her Lap, About it before ſhe weepe her ſelfe to a dry ground, And whine out all her goodneſſe. Nay and you'le follow my ſuit, & ſaue my purſe too Fortune doats on me, he's in happy caſe Finds ſuch an honeſt friend i'the Common place. Why there thou haſt it right, I looke for her this Euening Brother. I will deliuer you of the wonder ſtreight Brother, By the firme ſecreſie, and kind aſſiſtance Of a good Wench i'the Houſe, who made of pittie, Weighing the caſe her owne, ſhe's lead through Gutters, Strange hidden wayes, which none but Loue could find, Or ha' the Heart to venture, I expect her Where you would little thinke. Hope telles me ſo, But from your loue and time my peace muſt grow. I loue them with my Heart for't. Barne-Elmes. Goe, and you honeſt watermen that ſtay, Here's a French-crowne for you, There comes a Mayd with all ſpeed to take water, Row her luſtily to Barne-Elmes after me. What made you ſtay ſo long? Away quicke, there's a Boat waites for you, And I'le take water at Pauls-wharfe, and ouer-take you. O thy newes ſplits me. Enough, leaue me like my Ioyes, Sir ſaw you not a wretched Mayd paſſe this way? Heart Villaine, is it thou? I muſt breake through thee then, there is no ſtop That checkes my Tongue, and all my hopefull fortunes, That Breaſt excepted, and I muſt haue way. Sir you'le gaine the Heart in my Breſt at firſt? O now 'tis quit Sir. No longer Slaue? But one bout? I'le follow thee to death, but ha't out. My ioy wants vtterance.
What Dauy Dahanna, well-come from North Wales I faith, and is S r Walter come? Into the Mayds ſweet Dauy, and giue order his Chamber be made ready inſtantly, my Wife's as great as ſhe can wallow Dauy, and longs for nothing but pickled Coucombers, and his comming, and now ſhe ſhall ha'te Boy. Thy verie ſight will hold my Wife in pleaſure, till the Knight come himſelfe. Goin, in, in Dauy. The Founders come to Towne, I am like a Man finding a Table furniſh't to his hand, as mine is ſtill to me, prayes for the Founder, bleſſe the right Worſhipfull, the good Founders life. I thanke him, h'as maintain'd my Houſe this ten yeeres, not onely keepes my Wife, but a keepes me, and all my Family, I am at his Table, he gets me all my Children, and payes the Nurſe, monthly, or weekely, puts me to nothing, rent, nor Church duties, not ſo much as the Scauenger, the happieſt ſtate that euer Man was borne to. I walke out in a morning, come to breake-faſt, Find excellent Cheere, a good Fier in Winter, Looke in my Coale-houſe about Midſommer-eeue, That's full, fiue or ſixe Chaldorne, new layd vp, Looke in my backe yeard, I ſhall find a ſteeple Made vp with Kentiſh Fagot's, which o're-lookes The Water-Houſe and the Wind-milles, I ſay nothing But ſmile, and pin the doore, when ſhe lyes in, As now ſhe's euen vpon the point of grunting, A Lady lyes not in like her, there's her imboſſings, Embrodring, ſpanglings, and I know not what, As if ſhe lay withall the gaudy Shops In Greſſams Burſſe about her, then her reſtoratiues, Able to ſet vp a young Pothecarie, And richly ſtocke, the Foreman of a Drug-ſhop. Her Sugar by whole Loaues, her Wines by Rundlets. I ſee theſe things, but like a happy Man, I pay for none at all, yet Fooles think's mine, I haue the name, and in his Gold I ſhine. And where ſome Merchants would in Soule kiſſe Hell, To buy a Paradice for their Wines, and dye Their Conſcience in the Bloods of prodigall Heires, To decke their Night-peece, yet all this being done, Eaten with iealouſie to the inmoſt Bone, As what affliction Nature more conſtraynes, Then feed the Wife plumpe, for anothers veynes. Theſe torments ſtand I freed of, I am as cleere From iealouſie of a Wife, as from the charge. O two miraculous bleſſings, 'tis the Knight Hath tooke that labour, all out of my hands, I may ſit ſtill and play, he's iealouſe for me, Watches her ſteps, ſets ſpyes, I liue at eaſe, He has both the coſt and torment, when the ſtrings Of his Heart freats, I feed, laugh, or ſing, La dildo, dildo la dildo, la dildo dildo de dildo. Now Sirs, S r Walters come. Your Maſter, what am I? Pray am not I your Maſter? Ergo Knaue, your Maſter. Proud of your Worſhips health Sir. Eene after your owne making Sir, She's a tumbler a faith, the Noſe and Belly meets. At the good houre, they will and pleaſe your wor ſhip. I thanke your kind worſhip Sir. The game begins already. Now I muſt doe it, or he'le be as angry now, as if I had put it on at firſt bidding, 'tis but obſeruing, 'tis but obſeruing a Mans humour once, and he may ha' him by the Noſe all his life. His iealouſie begins, am not I happy now That can laugh inward whil'ſt his Marrow melts? Of my ſoule and conſcience Sir, ſhe's a Wife as honeſt of her Body to me, as any Lords proud Lady can be. No I proteſt Sir. O I beſeech you Sir, I'le ſtop that gap Where e're I find it open, I haue poyſoned His hopes in marriage already, Some old rich Widdowes, and ſome landed Virgines, And I'le fall to worke ſtill before I'le loſe him, He's yet too ſweet to part from. Ha Villaine, peace. Peace Baſtard, ſhould he heare em. 〈◊〉 are two fooliſh Children, they doe not know the Gentleman that ſits there. Where's your Legges Whore ſons? They ſhould kneele indeed if they could ſay their Prayers. True, and if ſhe beare a Male child, there's the Man in the Moone Sir. There was a Man, the Boy had neuer beene there elſe. No by my troth, I'le ſweare it's none of mine, let him that got it keepe it, thus doe I rid my ſelfe of feare, Lye ſoft, ſleepe hard, drinke Wine, and eat good cheere. I'le goe bid Goſſips preſently my ſelfe, That's all the worke I'le doe, nor need I ſtirre, But that it is my pleaſure to walke forth And ayre my ſelfe a little, I am ty'd to nothing In this buſineſſe, what I doe is meerely recreation, Not conſtraint. Here's running to and fro, Nurſe vpon Nurſe, Three Chare women, beſides maids & neighbors children. Fye, what a trouble haue I rid my Hands on, It makes me ſweat to thinke on't. I am going to bid Goſſips for your W ps child Sir, A goodly Girle I faith, giue you ioy on her, She looks as if ſhe had two thouſand pound to her portion And run away with a Taylor, A fine plumpe black ei'd ſlut, Vnder correction Sir, I take delight to ſee her: Nurſe. I call not you, I call the Wet Nurſe hither, Giue me the wet Nurſe, I 'tis thou, Come hither, come hither, Lets ſee her once againe; I cannot chuſe But buſſe her thrice an hower. Think'ſt thou ſo Nurſe, What ſayeſt to Wat and Nicke? Pup ſay'ſt thou me ſo, pup little Counteſſe, Faith Sir I thanke your Worſhip for this Girle, Ten thouſand times, and vpward. Here take her in Nurſe, wipe her, and giue her Spoone-meat. And now about theſe Goſſips. To your owne Child Sir? Troth I commend your care Sir, 'tis a thing That I ſhould ne're haue thought on. I am ſtudying who to get for Godmother Sutable to your Worſhip, Now I ha' thought on't. I'le fit your Worſhip then with a Male Partner. A kind proper Gentleman, Brother to M r Tuch wood. A neat Batchelor. In troth I pittie him, he ne're ſtands ſtill, Poore Knight what paines he takes, ſends this way one, That way another, has not an houres leaſure, I would not haue thy toyle, for all thy pleaſure, Ha, how now, what are theſe that ſtand ſo cloſe At the Street-corner, pricking vp their Eares, And ſnuffing vp their Noſes, like rich-mens Dogges When the firſt Courſe goes in? By the maſſe Promoters, 'Tis ſo I hold my life, and planted there To arreſt the dead Corps of poore Calues and Sheepe, Like rauenous Creditors, that will not ſuffer The Bodyes of their poore departed Debtors To goe to' th' graue, but eene in Death to vex And ſtay the Corps, with Billes of Middleſex, This Lent will fat the whoreſons vp with Sweetbreds, And lard their whores with Lambe-ſtones, what their gols Can clutch, goes preſently to their Mols and Dols, The Bawds will be ſo fat with what they earne, Their Chins will hang like Vdders, by Eaſter-eeue, And being ſtroak't, will giue the Milke of Witches, How did the Mungrels heare my wife lyes in? Well, I may baffle 'em gallantly, By your fauour Gentlemen I am a ſtranger both vnto the Citie, And to her carnall ſtricktneſſe. Pray tell me where one dwells that kils this Lent. Faith any Fleſh, But I long eſpecially for Veale and Greene-ſauce. I haue halfe a ſcornefull ſtomacke, no Fiſh will be admitted. Lent, what cares Colon here for Lent? That I was, I marry. Some Apple-loft as I take it, or a Cole-houſe, I know not which I faith. 'Tis a buſie day at our Houſe Dauy. Truſſe, truſſe me Dauy. How do's this Sute fit me Dauy? Thou haſt hit it right Dauy, We euer iumpt in one, this ten yeeres Dauy, So well ſaid, what art thou? O ſweet youth, into the Nurſe quicke, Quicke, 'tis time I faith, Your Miſtris will be here? There are ſome Wiues within, and ſome at home. Verily you are an Aſſe forſooth, I muſt ſit all theſe times, or there's no Muſicke, Here comes a friendly and familier payer, Now I like theſe Wenches well. They are pretie fooliſh things, Put to making in minutes, I ne're ſtand long about 'em, Will you walke in Wenches? Yes Sir, that's he muſt be your Worſhips Partner In this dayes buſineſſe, M r Tuchwoods Brother. Ready Sir. Why then ſo hope I too for company, I haue nothing to doe elſe. Well ſaid Nurſe, About, about with them amongſt the Goſſips, Now out comes all the taſſeld Handkerchers, They are ſpred abroad betweene their Knees already, Now in goes the long Fingers that are waſh't Some thrice a day in Vrin, my Wife vſes it, Now we ſhall haue ſuch pocketing, See how they lurch at the lower end. Againe, ſhe has taken twice already. A Pox it ſeemes your purity loues ſweet things well that puts in thrice together, had this beene all my coſt now I had beene beggerd, theſe Women haue no conſciences at ſweet meats, where e're they come, ſee and they haue not culd out all the long Plumbes too, they haue left nothing here but ſhort riggle-tayle-Comfits, not worth mouthing, no mar'le I heard a Citizen complaine once, that his Wiues Belly onely broke his Backe: Mine had beene all in fitters ſeuen yeeres ſince, but for this worthy Knight, that with a prop vpholds my Wife and me, and all my eſtate buried in Bucklers-berrie. Now the cups trole about to wet the goſſips whiſtles It poures downe I faith, they neuer thinke of payment. Now bleſſe thee, two at once, I'le ſtay no longer, It would kill me and if I pay'd for't, Will it pleaſe you to walke downe and leaue the women. Troth I cannot blame you. A Pox twice tipple ye, you are laſt & loweſt. Here's a noyſe, not parted yet? Hyda, a Looking-glaſſe, they haue drunke ſo hard in Plate, That ſome of them had need of other Veſſels, Yonder's the braueſt Shew. Come along preſently by the Piſſing-conduit, With two braue Drums and a Standert-bearer. You had more need to ſleepe then eat, Goe take a nap with ſome of the Brethren, goe, And riſe vp a well edified, boldified Siſter, O here's a day of toyle well paſt o're, Able to make a Citizen Hare mad, How hot they haue made the Roome with their thicke Bums, Do'ſt not feele it Dauy? What's here vnder the Stooles? Iſt no worſe think'ſt thou? Faire Needle worke Stooles, coſt nothing with them Dauy Looke how they haue layd them, Ee'ne as they lye themſelues, with their Heeles vp, How they haue ſhufflled vp the Ruſhes too Dauy With their ſhort figging little ſhittle-corke-heels, Theſe Women can let nothing ſtand as they find it, But what's the ſecret thou'ſt about to tell me My honeſt Dauy? Life rip my Belly vp to the Throat then Dauy. Marriage Dauy, ſend me to hanging rather. When, where, what is ſhe Dauy? I haue no time to ſtay, nor ſcarce can ſpeake, I'le ſtop thoſe wheeles, or all the worke will breake. The Yellowhammers in Oxfordſhiere, Neere Abbington. I hope the zeale I bring with me ſhall deſerue it. I vnderſtand by rumors, you haue a Daughter, Which my bold loue ſhall hence-forth title couſen. I heard of her vertues, and other confirm'd graces. Fame ſets her out with richer ornaments, Then you are pleas'd to boaſt of, 'Tis done modeſtly, I heare ſhe's towards marriage. And with a Knight in Towne, S r Walter Whore hound. I am the ſorrier for't. 'Tis not too farre paſt iſt? It may be yet recal'd? Reſolue me in that point ye ſhall heare from me. I am verie ioyfull Sir. By no meanes cus, ſhe's quite vndone then, And you'le curſe the time that e're you made the match, He's an arrant whoremaſter, conſumes his time and ſtate, —whom in my knowledge he hath kept this 7 yeres, Nay cus, an other Mans Wife too. Maintaines the whole houſe, apparels the husband, Payes ſeruants wadges, not ſo much, but — Knowes? I and glad he may too, 'tis his liuing, As other Trades thriue, Butchers by ſelling Fleſh, Poulters by venting Connies, or the like cous. Tuſh, what cares he for that? Beleeue me cous, no more then I doe. All's one to him, he feeds and takes his eaſe, Was ne're the Man that euer broake his ſleepe, To get a Child yet by his owne confeſſion, And yet his Wife has ſeuen. S r Walter 's like to keepe 'em, and maintaine 'em, In excellent faſhion, he dares doe no leſſe Sir. Children? Boyes thus high, In their Cato and Cordelius. Why, one can make a Verſe, And is now at Eaton Colledge. It had eaten neerer if it had not beene preuented. One Allwit 's Wife. I that worke did coſt the Knight aboue a hundred marke. Ha, ha, ha, this Knight will ſticke by my ribs ſtill, I ſhall not looſe him yet, no Wife will come, Where e're he woos, I find him ſtill at home, Ha, ha, What ſhall become of vs? Think'ſt thou ſo Dauy? Then am I mortall too, but a dead Man Dauy, This is no world for me, when e're he goes, I muſt e'ne truſſe vp all, and after him Dauy, A Sheet with two knots, and away. Hyday, my wife's layd downe too, here's like to be A good Houſe kept, when we are altogether downe, Take paynes with her good Dauy, cheere her vp there, Let me come to his Worſhip, let me come. He raues already, His ſences are quite gone, he knowes me not, Looke vp an't like your Worſhip, heaue thoſe Eyes, Call me to mind, is your remembrance loſt? Looke in my face, who am I an't like your Worſhip? Alas his poore Worſhips weakeneſſe, He will begin to know me by little and little. Ah poore Gentleman, Me thinkes the paine that thou endureſt. Now he is worſe and worſe, Wife, to him wife, thou waſt wont to doe good on him. Run ſweet Dauy quickly, And fetch the Children hither, ſight of them, Will make him cheerefull ſtraight. Speake to him Nicke. Tell him he hurts his wounds Wat, with making moane. Come let's be talking ſomewhat to keepe him aliue Ah ſira Wat, and did my Lord beſtow that Iewell on thee, For an Epiſtle thou mad'ſt in Latine, Thou art a good forward Boy, there's great ioy on thee. Heart will nothing comfort him? If he be ſo farre gone, 'tis time to moane, Here's Pen, and Incke, and Paper, and all things ready, Wil't pleaſe your Worſhip for to make your Will? That can your man Dauy an't like your Worſhip, A faire, faſt, legible Hand. How? Write them not downe Dauy. There's a ſweet Legacie, I am almoſt choak't with't. Let the Law lift you now, that muſt haue all, I haue done lifting on you, and my Wife too. Not in my Houſe Sir, I'le harbour no ſuch perſons as Men-ſlayers, Locke your ſelfe where you will. I know what I doe Wife. Away Wife, heare a Foole, his Lands will hang him. We neuer vſe, you forget ſickneſſe then, And Phyſicke times: Iſt not a place for eaſement? Harke you there Wife. I wonder what he makes here with his conſorts? Cannot our Houſe be priuate to our ſelues, But we muſt haue ſuch Gueſts? I pray depart Sirs, And take your Murtherer along with you, Good he were apprehended ere he goe, H'as kild ſome honeſt Gentleman, ſend for Officers. I muſt tell you Sir, You haue beene ſome-what boulder in my Houſe, Then I could well like of, I ſuffred you Till it ſtucke here at my Heart, I tell you truly I thought you had beene familiar with my Wife once. And therefore get you gone Sir. So, ſince he's like now to be rid of all, I am right glad, I am ſo well rid of him. That ſtop't his Spirits ſtraight, What ſhall we doe now Wife? We are richly furniſh't wife, with Houſhold-ſtuffe In troth a match Wench: We are ſimply ſtock't, with Cloath of Tiſſue Cuſſions, To furniſh out bay-windows: Puſh, what not that's queint And coſtly, from the top to the bottome: Life, for Furniture, we may lodge a Counteſſe: There's a Cloaſe-ſtoole of tawny Veluet too, Now I thinke on't Wife. I haue done Wench, And let this ſtand in euerie Gallants Chamber, There's no Gamſter like a politike ſinner, For who e're games, the Box is ſure a winner. See who comes here now.
speeches.1: What has he got a ſinging in his Head now? Is our Maſter come? Doe not you know Sir? O you are but our Miſtreſſes Husband. Negatur argumentum. Here comes S r Walter, now a ſtands bare as well as we, make the moſt of him he's but one peepe aboue a Seruingman, and ſo much his Hornes make him. Your firſt Man Sir. Your firſt man.
speeches.2: Now's out of worke he falles to making Dildo's. Shall I carrie you Gentlemen with a paire of Oares? Shall I carrie your Worſhip? To Barne-Elmes, good Sir: make ready the boat Sam, We'le wait below.
Sure Sir not any. Sir he can tell himſelfe.
Good Sir be patient. No liuing Creature entred. You will not heare me out Sir.
Sweet Knight Welcome, I haue all my longings now in Towne, Now well-come the good houre.
Made lightſome, eene by him that made me heauy. 'Twill be ſo tedious Sir to liue from you, But that neceſſitie muſt be obeyed. Sir for a time, I'le take the curteſie of my Vnkles Houſe If you be pleas'd to like on't, till proſperitie Looke with a friendly Eye vpon our ſtates. I ſhall not want your ſight? Your will be mine Sir. I, I thanke your paines. Sit downe good Neighbours, Nurſe. Looke they haue all low ſtooles Here M ris Yellowhammer, and Neighbours, To you all that haue taken paines with me, All the good Wiues at once. A miſerie of a Houſe.
I would it might not Wife, the tediouſneſſe Will be the moſt part mine, that vnderſtand The bleſſings I haue in thee, ſo to part That driues the torment to a knowing Heart, But as thou ſay'ſt, we muſt giue way to need All liue awhile aſunder, our deſires Are both too fruitfull for our barren fortunes. How aduers runs the deſteny of ſome Creatures, Some onely can get riches and no Children, We onely can get Children and no riches, Then 'tis the prudents part to checke our willes, And till our ſtate riſe, make our Bloods lye ſtill. 'Life euerie yeere a Child, and ſome yeeres two, Beſides, drinkings abroad, that's neuer reckon'd, This geere will not hold out. Honeſt Wife I thanke thee, I ne're knew The perfect treaſure thou brought'ſt with thee more Then at this inſtant minute. A Man's happy When he's at pooreſt that has match't his Soule As rightly as his Body. Had I married A ſenſuall Foole now, as 'tis hard to ſcape it 'Mongſt Gentlewomen of our time, ſhe would ha' hang'd About my Necke, and neuer left her hold Till ſhe had kiſt me into wanton buſineſſes, Which at the waking of my better Iudgement I ſhould haue curſt moſt bitterly, And layd a thicker vengance on my act Then miſerie of the Birth, which were enough If it were borne to greatneſſe, whereas mine Is ſure of beggerie, though it were got in Wine. Fulneſſe of Ioy ſheweth the goodneſſe in thee, Thou art a matchleſſe Wife, Farwell my Ioy. I'le ſee thee often, Talke in mirth, and play at kiſſes with thee, Any thing Wench but what may beget Beggers, There I giue o're the Set, throw downe the Cards, And dare not take them vp. This does not onely make her honeſtie perfect, But her diſcretion, and approues her Iudgement. Had her deſire beene wanton, they'd beene blameleſſe In being lawfull euer, but of all Creatures I hold that Wife a moſt vnmatched treaſure, That can vnto her fortunes fixe her pleaſure, And not vnto her Blood, this is like wedlocke, The feaſt of marriage is not Luſt but Loue, And care of the eſtate, when I pleaſe Blood, Meerely I ſing, and ſucke out others, then 'Tis many a wiſemans fault, but of all Men I am the moſt vnfortunate in that game That euer pleas'd both Genders, I ne're play'd yet Vnder a Baſtard, the poore Wenches curſſe me To the Pit where e're I come, they were ne're ſerued ſo, But vs'd to haue more words then one to a bargaine, I haue ſuch a fatall Finger in ſuch buſineſſe I muſt forth with't, chiefely for Countrey Wenches, For euerie Harueſt I ſhall hinder Hay-making, I had no leſſe then ſeuen lay in laſt Progreſſe, Within three weekes of one anothers time. How Snaphance? I'le haue the Parſons Hand too, or I'le not yeeld to't. Faith when ſhe will I'le haue a bout with her. True, Lawyers vſe ſuch bouts as other Men doe, And if that be all thy griefe, I'le tender her a Husband, I keepe of purpoſe two or three Gulls in pickle To eat ſuch Mutten with, and ſhe ſhall chuſe one. Doe but in courteſie faith Wench excuſe me, Of this halfe yeard of Fleſh, in which I thinke it wants A Nayle or two. Faith I am poore, doe a charitable deed Wench, I am a younger Brother, and haue nothing. I haue no dwelling, I brake vp Houſe but this morning, Pray thee pittie me, I am a good Fellow, faith haue beene too kind To people of your Gender, if I ha'te Without my Belly, none of your Sexe ſhall want it, That word has beene of force to moue a Woman. There's trickes enough to rid thy Hand on't Wench, Some rich-mans Porch, to morrow before day, Or elſe anone i'the euening, twentie deuiſes, Here's all I haue, I faith, take purſe and all, And would I were rid of all the Ware i'the Shop ſo. And I proteſt Wench, the next I'le keepe my ſelfe. what ſhift ſhele make now with this peece of fleſh In this ſtrict time of Lent, I cannot imagine, Fleſh dare not peepe abroad now, I haue knowne This Citie now aboue this ſeuen yeers, But I proteſt in better ſtate of gouernement, I neuer knew it yet, nor euer heard of, There has beene more religious wholeſome Lawes In the halfe cirkle of a yeere erected For common good, then memorie euer knew of, Setting apart corruption of Promoters, And other poyſonous Officers that infect And with a venemous breath taint euerie goodneſſe. What's here to doe now? I hold my life ſhe's in deepe paſſion For the impriſonment of Veale and Mutton Now kept in Garets, weepes for ſome Calues Head now, Me thinkes her Husbands Head might ſerue with Bacon. Why what's the buſineſſe? How, a Licence? Nay ſure thou ſhalt not miſſe ſo faire a marke ▪ For thirteene ſhillings foure pence. Quicke, make haſt Sirs. He can tell that as well as I. Looke after him and ſpare not, there he walkes That neuer yet receiued baffling, you'r bleſt More then e're I knew, goe take your reſt. Prethe ceaſe, I find a too much aptneſs in my blood For ſuch a buſineſſe without prouocation, You might 'well ſpar'd this banket of Oringoes, Hartechokes, Potatoes, and your butter'd Crabbe, They were fitter kept for your owne wedding dinner. Life what makes thee ſo merry? thou haſt no cauſe That I could heare of lately ſince thy croſſes, Vnleſſe there be newes come, with new additions. How's that, looke for her? I care not where, ſo ſhe be ſafe, and yours. You know the worſt then brother, now to my Kix The barren he and ſhe, they're i'the next Roome, But to ſay which of their two humors hold them Now at this inſtant, I cannot ſay truly. O iſt that time of day, giue you ioy of your tongue There's nothing elſe good in you, this their life The whole day from eyes open to eyes ſhut, Kiſſing or ſcolding, and then muſt be made friends, Then rayle the ſecond part of the firſt fit out, And then be pleas'd againe, no Man knowes which way, Fall out like Giants, and fall in like Children, Their Fruit can witneſſe as much. Pray ceaſe, When there are friendlier courſes tooke for you, To get and multiply within your Houſe, At your owne proper coſts in ſpight of cenſure, Me thinkes an honeſt peace might be eſtabliſh't. Sweet Sir. Let me intreat Sir. Iſt come to that, the peale begins to ceaſe. Some would thinke this impoſſible to compaſſe, Pray let this ſtorme fly ouer. Lady friends come? Can any man tell now which way they came in? By this light I'le be hang'd then. Here's a little Viall of Almond-milke That ſtood me in ſome three pence. By this light they are out againe at the ſame dore, And no Man can tell which way, Come here's your Drinke Sir. Then you muſt ride vpon't fiue houres. Stirre vp and downe ſir, you muſt not ſtand. So much the better ſir for the — O paſſing good Sir, and would ſhew well a Horſe backe: When you come to your Inne, If you leapt ouer a ioynt-ſtoole or two, 'twere not amiſſe although you brake your necke Sir. Nothing better Sir, if it be furniſhed with good Victuals. You remember how the bargaine runs about this buſineſſe? Right, that I haue Sir. All this is euen ſtill, a little faſter Sir. By this light they haue forgot their anger ſince, And are as farre in againe as e're they were, Which way the Diuell came they, Haart I ſaw 'em not, Their wayes are beyond finding out. Come ſweet Lady. Cleane contrarie, yours muſt be taken lying. A Bed, or where you will for your owne eaſe, Your Coach will ſerue. I had beene taken Brother by eight Sergeants, But for the honeſt Watermen, I am bound to them, They are the moſt requiteful'ſt people liuing, For as they get their meanes by Gentlemen, They are ſtill the forwardeſt to helpe Gentlemen, You heard how one ſcap't out of the Blacke-Fryers, But a while ſince from two or three Varlets Came into the Houſe with all their Rapiers drawne, As if they'd daunce the Sword-dance on the Stage, With Candles in their Hands like Chandlers Ghoſts, Whil'ſt the poore Gentleman ſo purſued and banded, Was by an honeſt paire of Oares ſafely landed. Theſe be the honeſt Fellowes, Take one paire, and leaue the reſt for her. No more Brother. By your leaue Sir. I may be now admitted, tho the Brother Of him your hate purſude, it ſpreads no further, Your malice ſets in death, does it not Sir? He's dead: 'twas a deere Loue to him, It coſt him but his life, that was all Sir: He pay'd enough, poore Gentleman, for his Loue. That helpt him forward, I muſt needs confeſſe: But the reſtraint of Loue, and your vnkindneſſe, Thoſe were the wounds, that from his Heart drew Blood, But being paſt helpe, let words forget it too: Scarcely three Minutes, ere his Eye-lids clos'd, And tooke eternall leaue of this Worlds light, He wrot this Letter, which by Oath he bound me, To giue to her owne Hands, that's all my buſineſſe. O with a following looke. Here's ſome Gold, He wil'd me to diſtribute faithfully amongſt your Seruants. How cheere you Miſtris? Here's a Letter from a Friend of yours, And where that fayles, in ſatisfaction I haue a ſad Tongue ready to ſupply. Seldome better, h'as a contented health now. Faith feeles no paine at all, he's dead ſweet Miſtris. As good now then, as let here lye in torment, And then breake it. This is ſhe that help't her ſtill, I'ue a reward here for thee Stay, let me helpe thee, 'tis the laſt cold kindneſſe I can performe for my ſweet Brothers ſake. Neuer could Death boaſt of a richer prize From the firſt Parent, let the World bring forth A paire of truer Hearts, to ſpeake but truth Of this departed Gentleman, in a Brother, Might by hard cenſure, be call'd flatterie, Which makes me rather, ſilent in his right, Then ſo to be deliuer'd to the thoughts, Of any enuious hearer, ſtaru'd in vertue, And therefore pining to heare others thriue. But for this Mayd, whom Enuy cannot hurt With all her Poyſons, hauing left to Ages, The true, chaſt Monument of her liuing name, Which no time can deface, I ſay of her The full truth freely, without feare of cenſure What Nature could there ſhine, that might redeeme Perfection home to Woman, but in her Was fully glorious, bewtie ſet in goodneſſe Speakes what ſhe was, that Iewell ſo infixt, There was no want of any thing of life, To make theſe vertuous preſidents, Man and Wife. I cannot thinke, there's any one amongſt you, In this full faire aſſembly, Mayd, Man, or Wife, Whoſe Heart would not haue ſprung with ioy & gladneſſe To haue ſeene their marriage day? Vp then a pace, and take your fortunes, Make theſe ioyfull Hearts, here's none but Friends. Nay, do not hinder 'em now, ſtand from about 'em, If ſhe be caught againe, and haue this time, I'le nere plot further for 'em, nor this honeſt chambermaid That helpt all at a puſh. Good Sir a pace. Here's a thing trould nimbly. Giue you ioy brother Were't not better thou ſhould'ſt haue her, Then the Mayd ſhould dye? Here be your Wedding Sheets you brought along with you, you may both goe to Bed when you pleaſe too. Vtter all at night then Brother. Siſter, delight will ſilence any Woman, But you'le find your Tongue againe, among Mayd Seruants, Now you keepe Houſe, Siſter. To tell you the full ſtorie of this Chamber-Mayd, And of her kindneſſe in this buſineſſe to vs, 'Twould aske an houres diſcourſe: In briefe 'twas ſhe, That wrought it to this purpoſe cunningly. A ſtorme, a ſtorme, but we are ſheltred for it. Here's a ſtrange day againe. Say you ſo Sir? Take heed how you dare a Man, while you liue Sir That has good skill at his Weapon.
O Snaphance, haue I found you. Doe you ſee your workemanſhip, Nay turne not from it, nor offer to eſcape, for if you doe, I'le cry it through the Streets, and follow you. Your name may well be called Tuchwood, a Pox on you, You doe but touch and take, thou haſt vndone me, I was a Mayd before, I can bring a Certificate for it, From both the Church-Wardens. Thou ſhalt haue more thou Villaine, nothing grieues me, but Ellen my poore couſen in Darbiſhiere, thou haſt crack't her marriage quite, ſhe'le haue a bout with thee. A Law bout Sir I meane. No, thou ſhalt find Villaine It hath right ſhape, and all the Nayles it ſhould haue. Nothing, thou haſt too much thou lying villaine Vnleſſe thou wert more thankefull. Where I find manly dealings I am pitifull, This ſhall not trouble you. Soft, let it be got firſt. This is the fifth, if e're I venture more Where I now goe for a Mayd, may I ride for a Whore. Women had need of wit, if they'le ſhift here, And ſhe that hath wit, may ſhift any-where. O ſweet Gentlemen, I am a poore Seruant, Let me goe. O you vndoe me Sir, 'Tis for a welthy Gentlewoman that takes Phyſicke Sir, The Doctor do's allow my Miſtris Mutton, O as you tender the deere life of a Gentlewoman, I'le bring my Maſter to you, he ſhall ſhew you A true authoritie from the higher powers, And I'le run euerie foot. Will you ſweare then to me, To keepe it till I come. What ſay you Gentleman? Nay then I run Sir.
O that e're I was begot, or bred, or borne. Hiſt. All but in bleſſings, And there the Begger goes beyond vs. O, ô, ô, To be ſeuen yeeres a Wife and not a Child, ô not a Child. Can any Woman haue a greater cut? Giue me but thoſe good deeds, and I'le find Children. Thouly'ſt breuitie. Thou deſerueſt worſe. Thinke but vpon the goodly Lands and Liuings That's kept backe through want on't. 'Tis our dry barrenneſſe puffes vp S r Walter, None gets by your not-getting, but that Knight, He's made by th' meanes, and fats his fortunes, ſhortly In a great Dowry with a Gold-Smiths Daughter. I haue ſuffred a long time. Nay thee, thou deſertleſſe Slaue. Yes, to my much ioy, Euerie one gets before me, there's my Siſter Was married but at Bartholmew-eeue laſt, And ſhe can haue two Children at a birth, O one of them, one of them would ha' ſeru'd my turne. What ſay'ſt Iugg? What iſt Wench? His name ſweet Iugg? That ſhall you Husband. True ſweet Husband, There's Land to come, Put caſe his Water ſtands me In ſome fiue hundred pound a pint, 'Twill fetch a thouſand, and a Kerſten Soule. I'le about it. And that's worth all ſweet Husband. Mine, Drouth and coldneſſe? I barren, ó life that I durſt but ſpeake now, In mine owne Iuſtice, in mine owne Right, I barren, 'Twas otherwayes with me when I was at Court, I was ne're call'd ſo till I was married. Be hang'd, I need not wiſh it, That will come too ſoone to thee: I may ſay, Marriage and hanging goes by deſtiny, For all the goodneſſe I can find in't yet. Where be they? Then he doth all like thee. But indeed you came not ſo ſingle, When you came from Shipboard.
Be content ſweet Wife. Patience ſweet Wife. Nay pray thee ceaſe, I'le be at more coſt yet, Thou know'ſt we are rich enough. Sweet Wife haue patience. I know 'tis great, but what of that Wife? I cannot doe with all, there's things making By thine owne Doctors aduice at Poticaries, I ſpare for nothing Wife, no if the price Were fortie markes a ſpoone-full, I'de giue a thouſand pound to purchaſe fruitfulneſſe, 'Tis but bating ſo many good workes In the erecting of Bridewels and Spittle-houſes, And ſo fetch it vp againe, for hauing none I meane to make good deeds my Children. Hang thee, thou haſt had too many. O horrible, dar'ſt thou call me breuitie? Dar'ſt thou be ſo ſhort with me? Talke not on't pray thee, Thou'lt make me play the Woman, and weepe too. They may be all deceiued, Be but you patient Wife. Suffer thy Heart out, a Poxe ſuffer thee. Come, come, I ha' done, You'le to the Goſſiping of M r Allwits Child? Sorrow conſume thee, thou art ſtill croſſing me, And know'ſt my nature. O that, that, that or nothing. Iſt poſſible? I'le venture that I faith. No matter, what ſerues wealth for? Thou lyeſt Barrenneſſe. 'Tis thy fault. Thine, 'tis thou art barren. I'le be deuorc't. I'le giue vp Houſe, & keepe ſome fruitfull whore, Like an old Batcheler in a Tradſmans Chamber, She and her Children ſhall haue all. What with her? Neuer. You worke all in vaine. Singleneſſe confound her, I tooke her with one Smocke. Heart ſhe bit ſore there, Prethe make's friends. I'le ſell all at an Out-cry. Good Sir pardon me, I'me Maſter of this Houſe, Which I'le ſell preſently, I'le clap vp Billes this Euening. Thou art nothing of a Woman. Nay prethe what do'ſt meane? I faith thou art a good Soule, he lyes that ſayes it, Buſſe, buſſe, pretie Rogue. Is the Drinke come? I hope to ſee thee wench within theſe few yeeres, Cirkled with Children, pranking vp a Girle, And putting Iewels in their little Eares, Fine ſport I ſaith. A Pox on thee. I will not take it now Sir, And I were ſure to get three Boyes ere Midnight. Hang ſtrumpet, I will take it now in ſpight. I meane ſo, Within there? Saddle the white Mare, I'le take a Whore along, and ride to Ware. I'le plague you euerie way, Looke ye, doe you ſee, 'tis gone. I curſe and ſpare not now. Nay I'me not giuen to ſtanding. I neuer could ſtand long in one place yet, I learnt it of my Father, euer figient, How if I croſt this Sir? What ſay you to a Table thus high Sir? Or elſe I had a bad Head: you muſt receiue Sir foure hundred pounds of me at foure ſeuerall payments: One hundred pound now in hand. Another hundred when my Wifes is quicke: the third when ſhe's brought a bed: and the laſt hundred when the Child cryes, For if it ſhould be ſtill borne, it doth no good Sir. Not a whit Sir, I'me in an excellent pace for any Phyſicke, I ſhall vp preſently: One kiſſe, and farewell. Expect me about three. Ho my Wiues quickned, I am a Man for euer, I thinke I haue beſtur'd my ſtumps I faith: Run, get your Fellowes altogether inſtantly, Then to the Pariſh-Church, and ring the Belles. Vpon my loue I charge you Villaine, that you make a Bon-fier before the Doore at night. A thwacking one I charge you. Run, tell a hundred pound out for the Gentleman That gaue my Wife the Drinke, the firſt thing you doe. A bargaine, as our ioyes growes, We muſt remember ſtill from whence it flowes, Or elſe we proue vngratefull multiplyers: The Child is comming, and the Land comes after, The newes of this will make a poore S r Walter. I haue ſtrooke it home I faith. Both, goe both together? My Wife helpes the number then? Her Parents may haue ioyfull Hearts at this, I would not haue my crueltie ſo talk't on, To any Child of mine, for a Monopoly. Come, we'le ſee't. M r Tuchwood, hear'ſt thou this newes? I am ſo indeer'd to thee for my Wiues fruitfulneſſe, That I charge you both, your Wife and thee, To liue no more aſunder for the Worlds frownes, I haue Purſe, and Bed, and Bord for you: Be not afraid to goe to your buſineſſe roundly, Get Children, and I'le keepe them. Proue me, with three at a birth, & thou dar'ſt now. 'Foot, I dare you Sir.
O Miſtris, weeping or rayling, That's our Houſe harmony. The ſweeteſt newes. One M r Tuchwood, a fine Gentleman, But run behind-hand much with getting Children. Why Sir, he'le vndertake, Vſing that Water, within fifteene yeere, For all your wealth, to make you a poore Man, You ſhall ſo ſwarme with Children. But I muſt tell you firſt, he's very deere.

At hand forſooth. They haue forſooth. A Gentleman from Cambridge, I thinke it be your Soone forſooth. Your Mother will haue it ſo.
Good, Your will Sir? How kils? Come hither Dicke, A Bird, a Bird. Greene-Gooſe, you ſhall be ſau'ſt. Not this Lent Sir? You ſay well Sir, Good reaſon that the Colon of a Gentleman As you were lately pleas'd to terme your worſhip Sir, Should be fulfill'd with anſwerable food, To ſharpen Blood, delight Health, and tickle Nature, Were you directed hither to this Street Sir? That ſhall not ſerue your turn, what a Rogue's this, how cunningly he came ouer vs? By your leaue Sir, We muſt ſee what you haue vnder your Cloake there. No, doe you tell vs that, what makes this lumpe ſticke out then, we muſt ſee Sir. 'Tis all Veale. Let's ſhare this, and ſee what hap comes next then. Sir, by your fauour. Good M r Oliuer, cry thee mercie, I faith. What haſt thou there? Goe, goe, we ſee thee not, away, keepe cloſe, Heart let him paſſe, thou'lt neuer haue the wit To know our benefactors. 'Tis M. Beggerlands man the wealthy Merchant That is in fee with vs. You know he purchaſt the whole Lent together Gaue vs ten groats a peece on Aſh-wenſday. A Wench. Looke, looke, poore Foole, She has left the Rumpe vncouer'd too, More to betray her, this is like a Murdrer, That will out-face the deed with a bloody Band. You ſhall Wench, but this muſt ſtay with vs. Now by this light I will. And ne're returne I hope. Imprimis Sir, a good fat Loyne of Mutton, What comes next vnder this Cloath? Now for a quarter of Lambe. Done. By the maſſe I feele I haue loſt, 'Tis of more weight I faith. No faith, here's a Lambes Head, I feele that plainly, why yet win my wager. Swounds what's here? A Poxe of all diſſembling cunning Whores. What ſhal's doe? We might leaue it elſe. Halfe our gettings muſt run in Suger-ſope, And Nurſes wages now, beſides many a pound of Sope, And Tallow, we haue need to get Loynes of Mutton ſtill, To ſaue Suet to change for Candles. Prethe no more on't, There's time to get it vp, it is not come To Mid-Lent Sunday yet. Faith nor I neither. Well, what iſt?
What iſt that you would haue? And the Butcher belike Should kill, and ſell cloſe in ſome vpper Roome? Either will ſerue, This Butcher ſhall kifſe Newgate, leſſe he turne vp the Bottome of the Pocket of his Apron, You goe to ſeeke him? Huſht, ſtand cloſe. O we loue that ſight well, you cannot pleaſe vs better: What doe you gull vs, call you theſe Shirts and Smockes? All Veale, Poxe the worſe lucke, I promis'd faithfully to ſend this morning a fat quarter of Lambe, to a kind Gentlewoman in Turnebull ſtreet that longs, and how I'me croſt. Agreed, ſtand cloſe againe, another bootie, What's he? I haue forgot him. Now I haue a feeling of him. True, true. Why then ſtand cloſe indeed. What time of the yeere iſt Siſter? Well, leaue your Basket then, And run and ſpare not. What a ſtrange Wench 'tis? Would we might periſh elſe. A politike Baggage, She makes vs ſweare to keepe it, I prethe looke what market ſhe hath made. Not for a Shoulder of Mutton. Why done Sir. Some Loyne of Veale? Ha? A Child. Here's an vnlucky Breakefaſt. The Queane made vs ſweare to keepe it too. Villanous ſtrange, 'Life had ſhe none to gull, but poore Promoters, That watch hard for a liuing. Nothing mads me, but this was a Lamb • head with you, you felt it, ſhe has made Calues heads of vs. I am ſo angry, I'le watch no more to day. Why then I'le make a motion. Let's e'ne goe to the Checker at Queene-hiue and roſt the Loyne of Mutton, till young Flood, then ſend the Child to Branford.
speeches.All: Where you ſhall not find him, I'le buy, walke by your Noſes with my Fleſh, Sheepe-biting Mungrels, Hand-basket Free-booters, My Wife lyes in, a footra for Promoters. Ne're more pittie. It would haue made a thouſand ioyfull Hearts. Aliue Sir? ô ſweet deere Couple. Ioy, ioy to you both. Neuer was houre, ſo fild with ioy and wonder. We ſhall all loue her for't. A Whore?
speeches.Man: I haue ſcap't well thus farre, they ſay the Knaues are wondrous hot and buſie. Haue? I haue nothing. What will you ſee Sir, a paire of Sheets, and two of my Wiues foule Smocks, going to the Waſhers? Now a Poxe choake you, You haue cozend me and fiue of my Wiues kinred Of a good Dinner, we muſt make it vp now With Herrings and Milke-potage. Meaning me Sir?
A Racke of Mutton Sir, and halfe a Lambe, You know my Miſtriſſes dyet.
speeches.Dauy: Alwayes the Kurſning day Sir. No matter and you were hang'd Sir. Excellent neatly, my Maſters things were euer fit for you Sir, e'ne to a Haire you know. I as a Man can get, And that's my Maſter. Into one Cup, moſt proper, A fitting complement for a Gold-ſmiths Daughter. I thinke his wound be mortall. O ſee Sir, How faint he goes, two of my Fellowes lead him. There are the children Sir, an't like your worſhip, Your laſt fine Girle, in troth ſhe ſmiles, Looke, looke, in faith Sir. It is his Will, I muſt. Of all Wittalles, Be thou the Head. Thou the grand whore of Spittles.
Your Comfit-makers Man Sir. She was ſetting forth Sir. Sir? Your white Mares ready. Where's the Knight? O Sir, the Gentleman you wounded, is newly departed. You were beſt locke your ſelfe cloſe. Troth worſe & worſe, you'r like to loſe your land If the Law ſaue your life Sir, or the Surgeon. S r Oliuer Kixes Wife is new quickned, That Child vndoes you Sir. It ſhall be done Sir. A Bon-fier Sir? This is monſtrous. A hundred pounds Sir? That you haue marry Sir. But will not your Worſhip goe to the Funerall Of both theſe Louers? I Sir, the Gentlemans Brother will haue it ſo, 'Twill be the pittifulleſt ſight, there's ſuch running, Such rumours, and ſuch throngs, a paire of Louers Had neuer more ſpectators, more Mens pitties, Or Womens wet Eyes. There's ſuch drawing out of Handkerchers, And thoſe that haue no Handkerchers, lift vp Aprons. I beleeue you Sir. 'Tis caſt ſo too, that both their Coffins meet, Which will be lamentable.
Giue you ioy of your fine Girle Sir, Grant that her education may be pure, And become one of the faithfull. Verily thankes Sir. Come ſweet Siſter, we goe in vnitie, and ſhew the fruits of peace like Children of the Spirit. Sure that was Iudas then with the red Beard.
Are any of the Brethrens Wiues yet come? I loue lowlineſſe. I would not feed my daughter with that ſpoone for all the World, for feare of colouring her Heyre, Red Hayre the Brethren like not, it conſumes them much, 'tis not the Siſters colour.
How do'ſt ſirra? Fye that thou'lt ſay ſo, Th'aſt as fine Children as a Man can get. Good M ris Yellowhammer. Indeed it ſhall be yours I'le ſtand ſtill then. You are ſuch another Creature. How iſt Woman, we haue brought you home A Kurſen Soule.
Want nothing, but ſuch getting Sir as thine. Before me, I pray come downe a little. Your place, great wonder ſure, are you any better then a Comfit-makers wife. Ye lye, yet I forbeare you too. Bring the Child hither Nurſe, how ſay you now Goſſip, iſt not a chopping Girle, ſo like the Father? The Mothers Mouth vp and downe, vp and downe. She had a ſore labour on't I warrant you, you can tell Neighbour. O here comes the chiefe Goſſip Neighbours. Calles vs all Ladyes. Me thinkes her Husband ſhewes like a Clowne to him. She's all fine Children Goſſip. Looke, looke, what has he giuen her, what Iſt Goſſip? Welcome from Cambridge.
Not a whit, I hope I know my place. And that's as good at all times as a Pothicaries. As if it had beene ſpit out of his Mouth, By'd, nos'd, and brow'd as like a Girle can be, Onely indeed it has the Mothers Mouth. 'Tis a large Child, ſhe's but a little Woman. O ſhe had great ſpeed, We were afrayd once, But ſhe made vs all haue ioyfull hearts againe, 'Tis a good Soule I faith, The Midwife found her a moſt cheerefull Daughter. O deer ſweet gentleman, what fine words he has The fatneſſe of our wiſhes. I would not care what Clowne my Husband were too, ſo I had ſuch fine Children. I, and ſee how faſt they come. Now by my faith a faire high ſtanding Cup, and two great Poſtle Spoones, one of them gilt. See Goſſip and ſhe lyes not in like a Counteſſe, Would I had ſuch a Husband for my Daughter. O no ſweet Goſſip. I that ſhe was laſt Lammas, But ſhe has a fault Goſſip, a ſecret fault. I'le tell you when I haue drunke. And now I'le tell you Goſſip, ſhe's too free. O I, ſhe cannot lye dry in her Bed. 'Tis as I tell you Goſſip. O bleſſe the Woman, M r Vnderman.
True, ſo ſay I, though they ſtriue more, There comes as proud behind, as goes before. I promiſe you a fine Gentleman, and a courteous. Is not ſhe toward marriage? Why ſhe's nineteene? A fault, what iſt? Wine can doe that I ſee, that friendſhip cannot. To free? What, and nineteene?
Yes, though I ne're was married Sir, I haue felt the force of loue from good mens daughters, And ſome that will be Mayds yet three yeeres hence. Haue you got a Licence? That's well. She ſhall be welcome Sir, I'le not be long A clapping you together. What's he? Then I'le not linger, Place that Ring vpon her Finger, This the Finger playes the part, Whoſe maſter Veine ſhoots from the Heart, Now ioyne Hands.
And verily well kurſend, i'the right way, Without Idolatry or Superſtition, After the pure manner of Amſterdam. No beleeue me, a verie ſpynie Creature, but all hart, Well metteld, like the faithfull to endure Her tribulation here, and rayſe vp ſeed. 'Tis the ſpirit, the Siſters are all like her, Children are bleſſings, if they be got with zeale, By the Brethren, as I haue fiue at home. Come hither Nurſe. I had forgot a Siſters Child that's ſicke. I'le anſwer for them, They wiſh all health and ſtrength, And that you may couragiouſly goe forward, To performe the like and many ſuch, Like a true Siſter with Motherly bearing. Fill againe Nurſe. Thanke your Worſhip Sir. Bring hither that ſame Cup-Nurſe, I would faine driue away this hup Antichriſtian griefe. Let me come next, Welcome from the Welſpring of diſcipline, that waters all the Brethren. 'Tis but the common affliction of the faithfull, We muſt embrace our falles. Feed and grow ſtrong.
speeches.Wife: So I hope to good Sir. O you are at too much charge Sir. I thanke you all for your paynes. O me! How iſt with you Sir? He is loſt for euer. Why Husband. You cannot tell yet, For hauing kild the Man in his defence, Neither his Life, nor eſtate will be touch't Husband. Alas Sir, I am one that would haue all well, But muſt obey my Husband. Prethee Loue Let the poore Gentleman ſtay, being ſo ſore wounded, There's a cloſe Chamber at one end of the Garret We neuer vſe, let him haue that I prethee. With me? I'le ſee him hang'd firſt, I defie him, And all ſuch Gentlemen in the like extremitie. I knew he durſt not ſtay, when you nam'd Officers As we were wont to doe. Let's let out Lodgings then, And take a Houſe in the Strand. There's that ſhould be Sir, Your Noſe muſt be in euerie thing. To you ſweet Miſtris Bride. I knew he was paſt the beſt, when I gaue him ouer. What is become of him pray Sir?
Thanke your Worſhip Sir. Where? Where Sir? O Braue. Farwell ſweet Goſſip.
speeches.Lady: Is your Sonne come forſooth? 'Tis great ioy on yee. A marriage? 'Tis a great ſpoyle of youth indeed. You're welcome M r Tim. Doe thy worſt Slaue, Good ſweet Sir bring vs into loue againe. If e're ye lou'd Woman, talke not on't Sir, what friends with him? good faith do you think I'me mad with one that's ſcarce the hinder quarter of a Man? Would I were leſſe then nothing. I cannot pleaſe you. You care not for me. I had you beene ought Husband, It had beene done ere this time. Thou art a Grub to ſay ſo. Why there thou ſhew'ſt now of what breed thou com'ſt To hinder generation, O thou Villaine, That knowes how crookedly the World goes with vs, For want of Heires, yet put by all good fortune. Ride to the Diuel. A Pox goe with it. Thou ſhalt haue two Loue. With all my Heart Sweet. How muſt I take mine Sir? A Bed Sir? The Phyſicke muſt needs pleaſe. It makes a hundred weeping Eyes, ſweet Goſſip.
O, I'me betray'd. Mother you doe intreat like a freſh Woman, 'Tis againſt the Lawes of the Vniuerſitie, For any that has anſwered vnder Batchelor To thruſt 'mongſt married Wiues. Call vp my Tutor Mother, and I care not. I ha' not brought him vp, he ſtands at dore, Negatur, there's Logicke to begin with you Mother. Come I from Cambridge, and offer me ſix plumbs? Seru'd like a Child, When I haue anſwer'd vnder Batcheler? O monſtrous abſurditie, Ne're was the like in Cambridge ſince my time, 'Life whip a Batcheler, yow'ld be laught at ſoundly, Let not my Tutor heare you, 'Twould be a Ieſt through the whole Vniuerſitie, No more words Mother. That did he Mother, but now I haue 'em all in my owne Pate, and can as well read 'em to others. Tim, harke you Timothius Mother, Timothius. O this is horrible, ſhe wets as ſhe kiſſes, Your Handkercher ſweet Tutor, to wipe them off, as faſt as they come on. This is intollerable, This woman has a villanous ſweet breath, did ſhe not ſtinke of Comfits, Helpe me ſweet Tutor, or I ſhall rub my Lips off. Perhaps that's the ſweeter, and we ſhall diſpatch the ſooner. Hoyſt I beſeech thee. I'me glad I ſcap't it, it was ſome rotten kiſſe ſure, It dropt downe before it came at me. Come Tutor. Negatur argumentum Tutor. Faller is ſane. Quomodo proba • domine. Sic argumentaris domine, ſtultus non habet rationem, ergo non eſt animal rationale, negatur argumentum againe Tutor. Participat. Ʋ t homo, probabo tibi in ſilagiſmo. Sic probo domine, ſtultus eſt homo ſicut tu & ego ſum, homo eſt animal rationele, ſicut ſtultus eſt animal rationale. Nothing but reaſoning about a Foole Mother. Why what's a Foole Mother? I come to you now. 'Tis prettie I faith, and well gueſt of a Woman neuer brought vp at the Vniuerſitie: but bring forth what Foole you will Mother, I'le proue him to be as reaſonable a Creature, as my ſelfe or my Tutor here. 'Tis the eaſieſt thing to proue a Foole by Logicke, By Logicke I'le proue any thing. I'le proue a Whore to be an honeſt Woman. 'Twill do't I tell you. Faith I can, and all their Daughters too, though they had three Baſtards. When comes your Taylor hither? By Logicke I'le proue him to be a Man, Let him come when he will. Piſh I made haberdins of 'em in Church porches Pox I haue it here now. Theſe women muſt haue all out. Grammatica? Ha, ha, ha. Are you not aſham'd Tutor, Gramatica? Why Recte ſcribendi at que loquendi ars, ſer-reuerence of my Mo ther. I mar'le what this Gentlewoman ſhould be, That I ſhould haue in marriage, ſhe's a ſtranger to me: I wonder what my Parents meane I faith, To match me with a ſtranger so: A Mayd that's neither kiſſe nor kin to me: Life doe they thinke I haue no more care of my Body, Then to lye with one that I ne're knew, A meere ſtranger, One that ne're went to Schoole with me neither, Nor euer play-fellowes together, They'r mightily o're-ſeene in't me thinkes, They ſay ſhe has Mountaines to her marriage, She's full of Cattell, ſome two thouſand Runts, Now what the meaning of theſe Runts ſhould be, My Tutor cannot tell me, I haue look't in Riders Dixcionarie for the Letter R, And there I can heare no tydings of theſe Runts neither, Vnleſſe they ſhould be Rumford Hogges, I know them not, And here ſhe comes, If I know what to ſay to her now In the way of marriage, I'me no Graduate, Me thinkes I faith 'tis bouldly done of her To come into my Chamber being but a ſtranger, She ſhall not ſay I'me ſo proud yet, but I'le ſpeake to her, Marry as I will order it, She ſhall take no hold of my words I'le warrant her, She lookes and makes a courſey, Salue tu quo que puella puleherima, Quid vis neſcio nec ſane curo, Tully 's owne phraſe to a Hart. Ferter me hercule tu virgo, Wallia vt opibus abundis maximis. I haue no Latine word now for their Runts, I'le make ſome ſhift or other: Itterum dico opibus abundat maximis montibus & fontibus & vt ita dicam Rontibus, atta men vero homauculus ego ſum natura ſimule arte bachalarius lecto profecto non parata. Cog foggin, I ſcorne to cog with her, I'le tell her ſo too in a word neere her owne Language: Ego non cogo. By my faith ſhe's a good ſcholler, I ſee that already She has the Tongues plaine, I hold my life ſhe has traueld, What will folkes ſay? There goes the learned couple, Faith if the truth were knowne, ſhe hath proceeded. I'me glad my Mothers come to part vs. As well as a Man might doe Mother, in modeſt Latine. And ſhe recoyl'd in Hebrew. All comes to one Mother. Who tould me ſo much? Heart and ſhe can ſpeake Engliſh, I'le clap to her, I thought you'ld marrie me to a ſtranger. O delicious, one may diſcouer her Countrey by her kiſſing, 'Tis a true ſaying, there's nothing taſts ſo ſweet as your Welch Mutton: It was reported you could ſing. And 'tis my mind I ſweare before I marrie, I would ſee all my Wiues good parts at once, To view how rich I were. I would not change my wife for a Kingdome, I can doe ſomewhat too in my owne Lodging. Theeues, Theeues, my Siſter's ſtolne, Some Thiefe hath got her: O how myraculouſly did my Fathers Plate ſcape, 'Twas all left out Tutor. Beſides three chaines of Pearle & a Box of Curral. My Siſter's gone, let's looke at Trig-ſtaires for her, My Mother's gone to lay the Common-ſtaires, At Puddle-wharfe, and at the Docke below, Stands my poore ſilly Father, Run ſweet Tutor, run. That's a buffe Serieant Tutor, he'le ne're were out. With Padlockes Father, the Venetian vſes it, My Tutor reads it. He ſayes true Father, a wiſe man for loue will ſeeke euerie hole: my Tutor knowes it. Dicit Virgillius Father. Run mad I thinke, I thought ſhe would haue drown'd her ſelfe, ſhe would not ſtay for Oares, but tooke a Smelt-boat: ſure I thinke ſhe be gone a fiſhing for her. Looke on her Tutor, ſhe hath brought her from the Water like a Mermayd, ſhe's but halfe my Siſter now, as farre as the Fleſh goes, the reſt may be ſold to Fiſh wiues. Why Father, my Tutor and I will both watch in Armour. Take you no care for that, if need be I can ſend for conquering mettall Tutor, ne're loſt day yet, 'tis but at Weſtminſter, I am acquainted with him that keepes the Monuments, I can borrow Harry the Fifth's Sword, 'twill ſerue vs both to watch with. Faith buſie Mother about an Epitaph, Vpon my Siſters death. No: but ſhe meanes to be, and that's as good, And when a thing's done, 'tis done, You taught me that Mother. Making one too, in principall pure Latine, Cul'd out of Ouid de Triſtibus. Chang'd? Gold into white Money was neuer ſo chang'd, As is my Siſters colour into paleneſſe. Lookes ſhe like Death, and ne're a word made yet, I muſt goe beat my Braines againſt a Bed-poſt, And get before my Tutor. Come from the Vniuerſitie, To marry a Whore in London, with my Tutor too? O Tempora! O Mors! I bought a Iade at Cambridge, I'e let her out to execution Tutor, For eighteene pence a day, or Brainford Horſe-races, She'le ſerue to carrie ſeuen Miles out of Towne well. Where be theſe Mountaines? I was promis'd Mountaines, But there's ſuch a Miſt, I can ſee none of 'em. What are become of thoſe two thouſand Runts? Let's haue about with them in the meane time. A Vengeance Runt thee. Troth I thanke you. I grant you I may proue another Mans Wife ſo, But not mine owne. Why then my Tutor and I will about her, As well as we can. Ʋ xor non eſt Meritrix, ergo falacis. I perceiue then a Woman may be honeſt according to the Engliſh Print, when ſhe is a Whore in the Latine. So much for Marriage and Logicke. I'le loue her for her Wit, I'le picke out my Runts there: And for my Moun taines, I'le mount vpon —

speeches.S. Ol: Had I bin ought, hang thee, had'ſt thou bin ought, But a croſſe thing I euer found thee.
I know not what he meanes, A Sutor quoth a? I hold my life he vnderſtands no Engliſh. What's this fertur and abundundis? He mockes me ſure, and calles me a bundle of Farts. This is moſt ſtrange, may be he can ſpeake Welch, Auedera whee comrage, der due cog foginis. Rhegoſin a whiggin harle ron corid ambre. As well as e're we did before we met. You put me to a Man I vnderſtand not, Your Sonne's no Engliſh Man me thinkes. I ha' been long enough in the chamber with him, And I find neither Welch nor Engliſh in him. 'Tis quickly pardon'd forſooth. Nay good ſweet Tim. Sir if your Logicke cannot proue me honeſt, There's a thing call'd Marriage, and that makes me honeſt.
Good Miſtris ſpare her. You are a cruell Mother. Halfe drown'd, ſhe cruelly tug'd her by the Hayre, Forc't her diſgracefully, not like a Mother.
No Diuell can be like thee.
speeches.Nicke: I dare not, I am afraid.
Great pittie of their deathes. I thinke we rid our Hands in good time of him.
Hands ioyne now, but Hearts for euer, Which no Parents mood ſhall ſeuer. You ſhall forſake all Widowes, Wiues, and Mayds: You, Lords, Knights, Gentlemen, and Men of Trades: And if in haſt, any Article miſſes, Goe inter-line it with a brace of kiſſes.
